13128-corea-or-cho-sen-the-land-of-the-m:
A. Henry Savage-Landor's 1895 travel book on Korea, then called Corea or Cho-sen, draws on his own drawings and journeys. He dedicates it to Queen Victoria and moves from Christmas aboard ship at Fusan through Chemulpo to Seoul and the court. Chapters cover cotton, body-snatching tales, hotels, Japanese concessions, and Korean history.

Savage-Landor recounts a tug-of-war over a child, sedan chairs waiting for officials, and a prince's court where he removed his shoes before entering. His tone is that of a confident Victorian traveler, curious and often blunt. The book gives a detailed, if dated, view of Korea just before its world changed fast.
18714-abe-and-mawruss-being-further-adve:
Montague Glass returned to his famous partners in this 1911 Doubleday collection, further adventures of Potash and Perlmutter. Abe Potash and Morris Perlmutter run their showroom with endless talk, sharp bargains, and warm quarrels, rendered in the partners' own comic dialect.

Stories with titles like Sympathy, The Judgment of Paris, The Raincoat King, and Firing Miss Cohen follow them through customers, rivals, and family claims on their time and money. The opening tale turns on Abe's praise of a supposed philanthropist, which Mawruss gleefully cuts down to mere talkativeness. Glass makes business comedy from two men who can sell anything except, sometimes, each other.
20347-the-moving-picture-girls-snowbound:
Laura Lee Hope published The Moving Picture Girls Snowbound in 1914. Alice DeVere, rather plump, with dark brown hair and eyes, waits at home. Her fairness contrasts with her sister Ruth's looks, the book notes. Their father is more than an hour late from the moving picture studio.

He promised to be back at four, and now it is after five. The Moving Picture Girls act in early films while storms trap them. Snowbound tales strand their cast far from the studio's bright lights. Young readers get early cinema glamor mixed with winter adventure.
2289-rosmersholm:
Henrik Ibsen's Rosmersholm stages a political and moral crisis in a Norwegian manor haunted by its past. Johannes Rosmer, a former pastor, has left the church and embraced free thought, but guilt over his wife's death and the scheming of Rebecca West pull him toward ruin. Ibsen's four-act play works through whispers, confessions, and the weight of a house's traditions.

The drama's power lies in what is not said: old sins, hidden motives, and the price of a clear conscience. Rosmer and Rebecca's final walk to the millrace is among Ibsen's most famous closes. Readers of serious drama will find a play of great psychological depth.
23361-pe-re-antoine-s-date-palm:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich built this New Orleans tale around a tall date palm near the levee, by the old French cathedral in the Place d'Armes. Sir Charles Lyell had noted the tree, some seventy or eighty years old, planted in youth by Pere Antoine, a Catholic priest who guarded it in his will.

Aldrich traces the priest's later life, as the old man grew thin and dry, walking the streets like a mummy, and the Creole folk who recalled him. The palm, with its broad leaves in alien air, becomes a sign of faith, age, and rootedness far from home. The tale is short and wistful, blending local lore, a real tree, and a priest whose life seemed to mirror the plant he loved.
23741-david-malcolm:
Nelson Lloyd published David Malcolm with Scribner's in 1913, dedicating it to his wife Susanne Livingston Green Lloyd, who worked with him over its pages. Its narrator is David himself, an only child under a double portion of maternal care. The book opens with his mother warning him from the gate not to tumble into the water.

David, perched on the back of the off-wheeler with boyish self-assurance, folds his arms like a circus rider rather than hold the harness. A second warning follows, about rattlesnakes, and a surreptitious kick fails to move the horse. From such small boyhood scenes Lloyd builds a novel of growing up, family, and a young man's push toward self-reliance.
3818-by-reef-and-palm:
Louis Becke, once a trader running a cutter between Apia and Savaii, writes these South Sea tales from first hand knowledge. The introduction recalls October 1870 in Apia, Samoa, when German traders feared a French squadron and the beach still buzzed over the pirate Pease and the notorious Bully Hayes. Becke's stories follow traders, chiefs, and beachcombers through love, revenge, and sudden fortune.

Challis the doubter, Macy O'Shea's revenge, the rangers of Tia Kau, and Enderby's courtship fill the contents. A Gilbert Islands village scene shows how a name shouted through a town house stops all song. Becke writes plainly and without polish, which suits his rough material. Readers who like island adventure will find a book salted with real Pacific life.
6863-the-passing-of-new-france-a-chronic:
William Wood tells the passing of New France in a chronicle of Montcalm, volume ten of the Chronicles of Canada, Toronto, 1915. War is the grave of the Montcalms, an old saying runs, as old as France herself, for Montcalm-Gozon men were always ready to fight for king and country. Montcalm, like Wolfe, was a soldier born, with ancestors famous in the Crusades.

Chapter one follows Montcalm in France from 1712 to 1756, before his Canadian campaigns and his death at Quebec. Wood writes with a historian's clarity and a storyteller's pace. The Passing of New France is a vivid, classic chronicle of a lost French empire.
7127-malcolm:
George MacDonald's Malcolm opens with a long roll of contents, from Miss Horn and Barbara Catanach through the mad laird, Phemy Mair, and Lady Florimel. Duncan MacPhail, Alexander Graham, the swivel, and the salmon trout follow, with a funeral, the old church, and the churchyard. The Marquis of Lossie, Meg Partan's lamp, the slope of the dune, and the storm lead to accusation, quarrel, and Duncan's pipes.

Advances, mediation, whence and whither, Armageddon, and the feast follow, with a night watch, not at church, and Lord Gernon. A fisher wedding, Florimel and Duncan, and a revival precede wandering stars, the skipper's chamber, and the library. Milton and the bay mare, Kirkbyres, the blow, and the cutter carry the tale toward Colonsay Castle and the deil's winnock.
abe-and-mawruss-being-further-adventures: Montague Glass tells further adventures of Potash and Perlmutter in Abe and Mawruss, published by Doubleday, Page in 1911. The contents run from Sympathy and The Judgment of Paris through Dead Men's Shoes and The Raincoat King to A Return to Arcady. A Present for Geigermann, Brothers All, and others follow, with Firing Miss Cohen, Aux Italiens, and Man Proposes closing the book. The frontispiece praises being up to date in business.
britannica-1911-balm:
Balm is a sweet-smelling herb, Melissa officinalis, of the deadnettle family. It has opposite, egg-shaped leaves with toothed edges, wrinkled on top, and small white or rose-spotted flowers. The plant is native to central and southern Europe.

Gardeners often grow it, and it has spread as a garden escape in the south of England and in North America. Its name comes from the Greek word for a bee, since bees visit it freely. The 1911 Britannica entry closes with a near kin, bastard balm, an allied plant of southern Europe also found in the south and south-west of England.
britannica-1911-bessel-friedrich-wilhelm:
Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel (1784–1846) was a German astronomer, born at Minden. At fifteen he entered a counting house at Bremen. Hopes of a post on a foreign voyage led him to navigation, mathematics, and astronomy. In 1804 he worked out the orbit of Halley's comet from old observations. Olbers printed the result and won him an observatory post at Lilienthal. A study of the comet of 1807 raised his name further.

In 1810 the king of Prussia called him to build a new observatory at Königsberg. He directed it from 1813 until his death. The 1911 Britannica entry credits him with opening the modern era of practical astronomy. He cut Bradley's Greenwich observations into a catalogue of 3,222 stars, the Fundamenta Astronomiae of 1818. His tables and perturbation studies fill the entry's close.
by-reef-and-palm:
Louis Becke, an Australian who traded among Pacific islands, gathered his stories in By Reef and Palm. An introduction recalls Apia in 1870, German traders, and Bully Hayes. Becke had sailed as supercargo, a ship's cargo officer, on Hayes's vessel and shared a shipwreck with him. The tales rest on that island knowledge.

Challis the Doubter opens the set, followed by a story of loyalty among islanders. The Revenge of Macy O'Shea and The Rangers of Tia Kau bring violence and justice to the beaches. Pallou's Taloi, Enderby's Courtship, and Long Charley's Good Little Wife mix love, custom, and comedy. A methodical trader of Majuru, a doctor's wife, and the fate of the Alida round out the volume. Brantley of Vahitahi closes the stories in the islands. Readers of Stevenson and Melville find a rawer Pacific, told by a working trader rather than a tourist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-culm:
A diocesan entry traces Culm, a bishopric in north-eastern Prussia founded in 1234 and suffragan to Gnesen. Land won by the Teutonic Order on the Vistula and Baltic was divided that year by papal legate William of Modena into four dioceses: Culm, Ermland, Pomesania, and Samland. Innocent IV consecrated the Dominican Heidenreich as first bishop in 1245.

The bishop held the highest spiritual and secular authority in his land, though dependent on the Teutonic Order. His chapter, founded in 1251, joined the Order under his successor. Under the Knights' protection, soil was tilled, inhabitants Christianized, and schools, churches, and courts founded. By 1907 the diocese counted 780,000 Catholics across West Prussia and neighbouring districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aldhelm:
St. Aldhelm was abbot of Malmesbury and bishop of Sherborne, Latin poet and church writer, living about 639 to 709. This entry follows a kinsman of Ine, King of Wessex, schooled at Malmesbury under the Irish teacher Maildubh. The town's very name is disputed between Maildubh and Aldhelm himself, perhaps honouring both.

Aldhelm credited his progress in letters to Adrian, the African-born monk of Monte Cassino who came to England with Archbishop Theodore and became abbot of St. Augustine's, Canterbury, though Theodore's arrival in 671 means Aldhelm was already thirty or forty. The entry follows his writings, his abbacy, and his bishopric, presenting a scholar who carried Latin learning into the West Saxon church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anselm:
St. Anselm was archbishop of Canterbury and a Doctor of the Church. He was born at Aosta, a Burgundian town on the borders of Lombardy. He died on 21 April 1109. This long entry follows a boy who learned his first lessons of piety from his mother, Ermenberga, of an old Burgundian family. His father Gundulf was a Lombard who had become a citizen of Aosta.

As a child Anselm heard his mother speak of God dwelling on high and ruling all things. Living among mountains, he imagined heaven must sit on their lofty summits. One night he dreamed he climbed to the summit and hastened to the court of God, the great King. His biographer Eadmer preserved such childhood memories from Anselm's own lips. The entry follows him from those early visions to the abbacy of Bec and the see of Canterbury, where his writings shaped medieval theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stockholm:
Stockholm, capital of Sweden, stands where Lake Mälaren meets a rocky Baltic bay. This entry surveys the city as it stood near 1910. It sketches the islands and heights it is built on, its founding tale under Birger Jarl, and its arms bearing King St Eric.

Trade figures for 1908 show a busy port, with hundreds of factories and tens of thousands of workers. Schools range from the free college founded in 1878 to the Caroline medical institute. Church life gets close attention too, with Catholic numbers, parishes, and the rule that Catholics sought marriage papers from Lutheran pastors. Statistics and sources round out the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edmund-br:
Edmund Brindholm, also spelled Bryndeholme, was a martyr and parish priest of Our Lady's at Calais, accused of plotting to betray Calais to the French. The tale ran that Sir Gregory Botolf, chaplain to Lord Lisle, Governor of Calais, had gone to Rome on the business. There he asked the pope to grant Brindholm a living in the English Hospital of St Thomas. Brindholm was about to leave for Rome when he was arrested.

No evidence seems to show he truly joined any plot. Examined on 11 April 1540, he was attainted in that year's Parliament with Clement Philpott of Calais. The charge was adhering to the king's enemy, the Bishop of Rome, and aiding Cardinal Pole in compassing the surprise of Calais. He suffered with Philpott, a victim of Henry VIII's treason laws rather than a proven conspirator, the entry argues.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BronsonFilm_Bro:
Charles L. Bronson stood in Dealey Plaza with a movie camera on November 22, 1963, and his film of the assassination slept for years before researchers examined it closely. Earl Golz of the Dallas Morning News reported on it in 1978, when enhanced frames made news.

The enhanced images appeared to show two figures in the Texas School Book Depository's sixth-floor window, where the Warren Commission had placed Oswald alone. If a second figure was real, the lone-gunman account had a problem, and the film became a battleground of photographic experts. Golz's article is the hometown paper covering the evidence debate as it heated up again in the seventies.
malcolm:
Malcolm is a Scottish novel by George MacDonald, set on the Moray coast. Its contents open with Miss Horn and the mad laird. Barbara Catanach, Phemy Mair, and Lady Florimel enter early. The Marquis of Lossie holds the great house above the fisher town.

Malcolm is a fisher lad who works the salmon nets and boats. Duncan MacPhail, a blind Highland piper, stands as his friend and guide. A funeral, a storm, and an accusation test the village. Weddings, revivals, and disclosures crowd the long tale. MacDonald hides a mystery of birth inside the fishing life. His deep faith and poetic heart shine through every chapter.
nasa-tm-19700020670-buoyancy-effects-on-:
S. S. Papell of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 cryogenic engineering conference in Boulder, Colorado. It studies how buoyancy affects film boiling of liquid nitrogen in vertical flow. In film boiling, a blanket of vapor wraps the heated surface.

Papell took data for flow moving both upward and downward. The tests ran through an electrically heated tube section. Pressures, inlet speeds, and heat levels all varied across the runs. How buoyant vapor moves against or with the flow changes the boiling. The results matter for cooling systems that carry very cold liquids.
podcast-dannyjones-v76xgCpW5LM:
Researcher Matthew Johnson joins Danny Jones to talk about a new test that uses religious drugs to try to bring God back. Johnson works on DMT and the strange worlds it opens. The test at issue gives the drug in slow, long doses.

Johnson explains how the test is run and what the subjects report at the peak. He asks whether the shared world they find could be a real place where God can be met. Jones presses on faith, fraud, and proof. Listeners get the science and the wonder in one talk. The library files it as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-EvnLN8WETlM:
Wildlife biologist Forrest Galante joins Joe Rogan for episode 2531 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Galante hosts Extinct or Alive, where he searches for animals thought to be gone forever. His adventures mix science, danger, and genuine discovery in remote places.

Galante tells tales of crocodiles, sharks, and close calls from his expeditions. He explains how his teams confirmed species that science had written off. Rogan, an avid outdoorsman, trades his own stories of the wild. Nature lovers and the brave get a front-row seat to a modern explorer's best missions.
rosmersholm:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Rosmersholm, a play in four acts, here in a translation by R. Farquharson Sharp. John Rosmer, of Rosmersholm, is an ex-clergyman who lives with Rebecca West, first hired as companion to the late Mrs. Rosmer. The cast also holds Kroll, headmaster of the local grammar school and Rosmer's brother-in-law, plus Ulrik Brendel, Peter Mortensgaard, and Mrs. Helseth, the housekeeper. The action takes place at an old manor house near a small town on a fjord in western Norway.

Act 1 opens in the sitting room at Rosmersholm on a summer evening after sunset. The room is large, furnished in old style, with portraits of clergy, officers, and officials on the walls. the-passing-of-new-france-a-chronicle-of:
William Wood wrote The Passing of New France, a chronicle of Montcalm. It is volume 10 of the Chronicles of Canada, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, published at Toronto in 1915. Chapter One covers Montcalm in France from 1712 to 1756. It opens with an old family saying: war is the grave of the Montcalms.

Wood traces the family back to the Crusades. Deodat de Gozon became Grand Master of the Knights of St John after devoted service. He won the right to bear the conquered Dragon of Rhodes on the family arms. Montcalm, like Wolfe, was a soldier born. Wood says the badge of victory nerved him to uphold the family tradition in Canada.
